name: Robotics

claims.claim_text: Early BeagleBoard projects clustered around robotics and machine vision, including autonomous flying vehicles that used a Kinect sensor with LibFreenect to build 3D maps and recognize faces.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's been a lot of cool robotic stuff. I think that's where you see most of the projects coming out, doing vision stuff. These autonomous drones. So you see these flying vehicles that go around and recognize objects and actually build out 3D maps.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jason Kridner - Bonafide BeagleBoard Bionomics

claims.claim_text: College programs began packaging robotics as mechatronics, deliberately combining electronics coursework with mechanical engineering rather than teaching either discipline alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a lot of college courses that now you know combine electronics with the mechanical mechatronics sort of you know aspects
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: A media-processing board can be repurposed as a robot controller by retrofitting motor controllers plus digital and analog I/O onto the existing design instead of starting a new platform from scratch.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's merged with a bunch of like motor controllers and digital IO, analog IO. So you can use it.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: A Linux single-board computer used as a robot controller has a practical development advantage over a bare microcontroller: you can attach a monitor and keyboard to bring the robot up, then run the same board headless in the field.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've got your little robot or something, you can plug a monitor and a keyboard into it, get it working, and then run it headless
claims.speaker: Eben Upton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: A drone company operating at the experimental edge of robotics accepts that its platform will be unstable; buyers who want stability should choose a consumer product and wait, while the company's actual customers demand the newest sensors and computing platforms.
claims.quote_verbatim: if what you want is stability and, you know, and such, then, you know, then you should, you know, buy a pair of AR – not you. One should buy a pair of AR drone and have fun for now and wait until things stabilize.
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: In robot builds the mechanical hardware is the easy half; without control software the actuators are inert, and generating human-like motion is an extremely hard control-systems problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: He said, the best hardware of the world is just dumb actuators if you don't have a mind to drive it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Surface-mount placement in contract assembly was heavily automated while reel loading and through-hole placement stayed manual, because robotics could not yet match human handling of those tactile steps.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think a lot of that stuff is still done manually because, you know, it, at a certain point in time, it, it's like, you know, I think robotics technology is just not there yet.
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: A position tracker built for another product can be split out and its raw ASCII position output left exposed so third parties can build robotics on top of it; hackability was the single most requested feature from makers.
claims.quote_verbatim: Maybe the tracker is something we split out and let people, uh, you know, do other stuff with. Number one feature requested Maker Faire, of course, is hackable, right?
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: A collection of research robots spanning the 1980s to the mid-2000s doubles as a survey of electronics construction technique: wire wrap, sockets with IDC backs jumpered in magnet wire, and point-to-point protoboard, with printed circuit boards only appearing by the mid-2000s.
claims.quote_verbatim: So like wire wrap and funky sockets that have IDC on the back of the socket. So you can use like magnet wire to connect sockets and, and like a lot of proto board and point to point wiring. And then, you know, you get into the mid 2000s and then people are starting to actually use printed circuit boards.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: FIRST Lego League competitions include a live-coding element where teams must modify their robot on the spot for changes they were not told about in advance.
claims.quote_verbatim: in first Lego League, a lot of the times there's like this like live coding piece where like you have to update your robot manually and you don't know what the changes are going to be
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: Warehouse robots that move whole shelves in a mixed human-robot environment are the deployed, revenue-generating end of practical robotics, in contrast to concepts that have only started up the hype curve.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have practical robotics in a, you know, a mixed human robotic environment. And I think that, that is very interesting right now. That's happening right now.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: Robotics is inherently a cross-disciplinary field spanning mechanical, electrical and software work, which is what draws people trained in one discipline into the other two.
claims.quote_verbatim: But I was always interested in robotics, which kind of covers a mix of fields, you know, mechanical, electrical, and software.
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: Even a large electronics distributor still uses human packers walking to shelves rather than robots retrieving bins, because replicating human picking ability at the cost of a wage is very hard.
claims.quote_verbatim: At least a robot to go and pull a box off the shelf that had that part. You know? And then it comes back to the operator. But no, the packer goes to the shelf and gets them.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: The PR2 research robot was developed by Willow Garage and runs the open-source Robot Operating System, which allowed outside groups to buy the hardware and develop applications such as laundry folding on top of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: so the pr2 is the uh it's a open source robot from well actually i don't know if the robot's open source uh but it uses the uh the open source robot operating system ross right ross yeah it's from uh i believe it's willow garage is the is the group that actually develops the hardware
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Guns and Mobile Labs - Nuanced Nomadic Non-essentials

claims.claim_text: Robotics and machine tools differ mainly in expected development cycle time: robotics assumes fast iteration while machine tools do not, which is why the same interfacing approach produces different outcomes in each domain.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's, like, a development cycle difference where robotics is something that is used to a quick development cycle. And machine tools are not used to a quick development cycle.
claims.speaker: Nadya Peek
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Robot Operating System at the time required ARMv7, so single-board computers with older ARM cores could not run it and boards moving to ARMv7 suddenly inherited the whole existing ARM software ecosystem.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm excited to see what, like, robot operating system is. Right. It only supports arm V7.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: Advances in prosthetic arms and robotics were attributed to the combination of cheap microprocessors and improved materials rather than to any single mechanical breakthrough.
claims.quote_verbatim: And robots, you know, because of the microprocessors, because of the ability that we've done with being able to build materials and things like that.
claims.speaker: Chuck Peddle
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Chuck Peddle - Charismatic Chipmaking Coryphaeus

claims.claim_text: The wave of consumer robot products was driven by cheap processing power for control systems, not by any improvement in motor or actuator technology.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's gotta be because, not because the, the motor and actuator technology and all that sort of jazz is getting any better. Right. It's all about control systems.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Robots are coming - Ominous Operational Overhaul

claims.claim_text: A small hardware manufacturer chose to automate garment production specifically to avoid depending on low-wage overseas labor, treating robotics as an ethical sourcing decision rather than only a cost one.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want to pay people low wages especially not, you know, somebody overseas low wages to put together clothing. I'm trying to do things a little bit differently. Try to make it as robotic as possible.
claims.speaker: Fabienne Serrière
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Fabienne Serrière of KnitYak

claims.claim_text: A $10 incremental bill-of-materials cost for a speech recognition module is negligible on a robotics project but prohibitive on a commodity appliance, and volumes in the millions cut the cost about 30 percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: so at $10, it's going to be adequate for some applications. But it's going to be way too expensive for other things
claims.speaker: Bertrand Irrisou
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bertrand Irrisou and Gerald Friedland of Audeme

claims.claim_text: Standardizing an ecosystem on a single connector and cable family concentrates volume on those parts, which is what drives the unit cost down.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're trying to consolidate, like, Seed Studio are trying to consolidate on this type of connector, right? And these cables, which is great, because then it allows you to get the volume
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Powered exoskeletons are an old concept whose recent feasibility came from real-time processing for sensor feedback and motor control plus falling cost, not from lighter motors or dramatically better batteries.
claims.quote_verbatim: the concept of an exoskeleton is not new at all. I think what it really is, it's just, we're starting to hit this, you know, this sweet spot of, you know, battery densities have gone up a little bit, but really more so... Process, real-time processing power for sensor feedback and motor control.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An assistive exoskeleton is not commanded with coordinates or inverse kinematics; gyros and other sensors detect the motion the wearer's limb is beginning to make and the actuators amplify it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're not typing in like coordinates or, or the, you know, the reverse kinematics, you know, that kind of stuff. You're, it's basically just sensing what you, you know, what your leg would be doing normally and then trying to amplify that and move it forward.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Even as global labor costs rise, a low-paid human worker still outpaces an expensive robot in many electronics assembly scenarios, which limits how fast collaborative robots displace assembly labor.
claims.quote_verbatim: even with the price of labor going up all over the world, you know, a low-paid person will outpace a high-paid robot in a lot of scenarios
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Making an animatronic limb move convincingly rather than jerkily depends on motor accuracy and mechanical tolerances as much as on the control software.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's definitely all about accuracy of motors and their tolerances. Okay. You know, if you don't want it to be jittery, if you want it to be smooth and precise control.
claims.speaker: Timothy Lamb

claims.claim_text: Announced factory automation programs targeted assembly and material handling rather than fine motor control tasks, so claims of wholesale worker replacement need to be checked against which operations are actually being automated.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think assembly and stuff like that. I mean, it's not going to be like fine motor control stuff yet, but it's, it's moving towards that way. And, you know, there's material handling stuff.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: Amazon paid roughly $750 million for Kiva, whose robots move shelves rather than pick items; picking itself stayed human because human dexterity remained far better, especially for ad hoc situations where something goes wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: there isn't that level of automation at the pick level yet and even amazon they don't have robots picking things because human dexterity is still better
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Sensor systems for self-driving vehicles were identified as a large near-term opportunity for electronics engineers, distinct from the automation of driving itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think sensor systems as well on, on, um, self-driving cars is a big field of opportunity for our listening audience
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Human operators remain necessary in otherwise autonomous systems precisely because robots handle unexpected situations poorly.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean you need the pilots for when unexpected things happen because that's where robots just don't do well. They can't today do things that's unexpected.
claims.speaker: Gerry Roston

claims.claim_text: LiDAR was described as possibly half of a robot's bill-of-materials cost at the time, with an expected fall to roughly five percent within five years, following the same cost curve Wi-Fi integration went through.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think in the article they talk about like it might be 50% of your bomb cost now, but it's probably going to be closer to five in, you know, in five years
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Building good robots remains hard enough that even state-of-the-art humanoid platforms fall over, a useful corrective to demo videos.
claims.quote_verbatim: One thing that has not changed is it's still hard to build good robots, right? Yeah, right. And even the best ones fall over, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Off-the-shelf CNC stepper shields expose only one global enable line, which blocks per-motor calibration routines and forces either a firmware workaround or a custom board.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need to disable each motor individually so I can do a separate calibration routine. And there's only one global, uh, on or off enable disable.
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: One builder deliberately avoided Robot Operating System because its abstraction layer obscured the stack he needed to understand end to end, from the browser issuing a command down to the motor executing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I look at Ross as kind of like this huge, uh, foggy, uh, window that I can't see through. Like they're purposely trying to create this abstraction layer
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: A robotic device-testing rig uses OpenCV against a video feed or camera to locate on-screen elements, convert them into targets, and then physically tap them.
claims.quote_verbatim: where I use the open CV library, I'm using either a video feed off the device or a camera. And then I'm using, uh, open computer vision magic to find elements on the screen, converting that to an element and then clicking that.
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Japanese robotics research long emphasized humanoid demonstration robots that could walk, dance and wave; after the Fukushima nuclear accident none of them could enter a reactor to locate fuel rods, and the research emphasis shifted.
claims.quote_verbatim: the kind of culturally embarrassing thing after Fukushima was that none of those robots could go into a nuclear reactor and, uh, you know, find the missing uranium rods, right?
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Choosing a hobby robot project for career value rather than utility changes the work: it justifies spending time on matrix math, kinematics and drive mechanisms you can explain in an interview, whereas a purely functional home project would not.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ability to identify and react to environmental stimulus through a robot in which I can explain the kinematics and the drive mechanisms, that's all career-wise very good for me

claims.claim_text: Supplier rating systems on manufacturing marketplaces are structurally unreliable, because a buyer who had a good project leaves five stars and a buyer who had a bad one silently walks away rather than damage a relationship they may need again.
claims.quote_verbatim: part of their core idea was like supplier ratings. And as a buyer, there's very little incentive for me to leave anything but a five star rating.
claims.speaker: Spencer Wright

claims.claim_text: 3D Robotics effectively exited drone hardware and became a software company after Chinese manufacturers drove component and product prices down faster than it could compete.
claims.quote_verbatim: 3d robotics is like out of the they don't make drones barely anymore i think they're a software company now
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The core problem shared by machining and robotics is establishing where objects are in free space relative to an origin; one indoor positioning approach projects a machine tool's coordinate frame out into 3D free space over a 10 meter radius of factory floor.
claims.quote_verbatim: we project that out onto the factory floor, 10 meters radius. That's what we do. We project it out in 3D, free space, out to 10 meters.
claims.speaker: Gregory Charvat
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies

claims.claim_text: A pick-and-place machine is a robot that needs per-component-type calibration and component libraries in addition to X-Y placement coordinates, so an unfamiliar part stalls the process.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a robot at the end of the day. So it needs to have calibration around component types and all the other things that are in there.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Introducing a previously unseen component into an assembly line remains a manual step, because someone must look up the datasheet and determine the physical package size before the machine can place it.
claims.quote_verbatim: a manual process because it still requires you looking up a data sheet and determining what size that component is and all that kind of stuff
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A legged robot can derive its kinematic model empirically: a springy tendon is wound up, a foot sensor detects ground contact, and the leg either complies or unwinds so the model is computed from where the leg actually ends up.
claims.quote_verbatim: That basically pulls up a springy tendon, and then has a foot sensor. And when it hits the ground, it either complies, or it unwinds the springy tendon. And then we can calculate the kinematic model from wherever the leg ends up, essentially.
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: Brushless motors deliver power densities that make legged robots practical: a two-kilowatt brushed DC motor is physically enormous, while the brushless equivalent is small for the same output.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you think about what a two kilowatt brushed motor would look like, a DC brushed motor, it's a massive thing. And these are, you know, relatively small for the power you get out of them
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: For robot joints, using an existing brushless controller such as ODrive beats rolling your own, because it is the one option aimed at robotics that handles accurate encoder-based positioning.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean, there are others around there, but this is the only one really that's meant for robotics that does the accurate encoder positioning.
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: Robotics is better understood as an approach to developing products and a toolset for solving problems than as an industry, which is why some problems call for it and others clearly do not.
claims.quote_verbatim: fundamentally robotics is not an industry. It's more of a approach to developing products, uh, and, you know, a tool set to use in solving problems
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: A fielded robot must simultaneously interact with people, move through the real world, carry its own power, be safe, be small enough to maneuver and big enough to be useful, which is a set of mutually incompatible constraints.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're making a system that has to interact with people, move around in the real world, bring its own power, be safe, be big enough to actually do something useful
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: The buy-versus-build calculation for a robot subsystem should be framed in engineer-months: a component that replaces four months of engineering and is guaranteed to work first time is worth buying so engineers can attack domain-specific problems instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I can buy a component that is four months of my time and it's guaranteed to work the first time, I, it's stupid not to do that
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: A shape memory alloy actuator can be built to produce linear motion with high force and precision, offering an alternative to conventional linear actuation approaches in mechatronic systems.
claims.quote_verbatim: pioneering a new type of mechatronics actuator or a driver that uses shape memory alloy that basically acts in a straight line or linear motion but can generate pretty amazing force and precision
claims.speaker: Dean Pick

claims.claim_text: An early-stage hardware investor's first working session covers market definition, what products already exist and how they work, which technologies could be the differentiator, and what technical moat prevents a copycat six months later.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll talk about like, what's the market who would want to buy this? What products exist out there? How do they work? What technologies do they use?
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Robotics and CNC use similar hardware but differ in required precision: a robot only needs to reach a target within an acceptable envelope and can close the loop with vision, while CNC must control every aspect of the path precisely.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're trying to get to a target, but you might not really care, you know, as long as it stays within an envelope that it gets there. So you could use vision, you know, to close the loop. But, uh, with CNC, you, you really have to precisely control every little aspect of it.
claims.speaker: Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Tasks whose target geometry varies each time, such as tying a shoelace, cannot be programmed as a fixed path and require the robot to sense the workpiece before deciding how to move.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're trying to get a robot to tie a shoe, you really can't program that. It needs to see the lace and, you know, how it's laying and things like that.
claims.speaker: Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Highly productive independent builders standardize on a small reusable toolbox of parts and techniques and apply it project after project, changing platforms rarely and deliberately.
claims.quote_verbatim: But he builds a skill or like a feature that he like uses over and over again. So it was like a big deal when he switched from like an Arduino Mega to like a Teensy. But he just keeps using it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The realistic near-term factory robot augments a worker rather than replacing them, taking over the heavy lifting that previously required extra co-workers while the human retains the decisions about stopping and moving.
claims.quote_verbatim: the robot at the factory might not do my entire thing but it might lift the heavy stuff that i had it took me you know two other co-workers to lift something up
claims.speaker: Craig J Bishop
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: An investment thesis in applied robotics was built by tracking falling component costs and asking which new solutions become possible in a one-to-five-year window when a technology cost change meets a market change.
claims.quote_verbatim: three or four years ago, we started looking at, at the lowered cost of a bunch of components and we said applied robotics, not the general purpose Jetson
claims.speaker: Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: The economically defensible robotics case is automating the simple repetitive portion of skilled work, such as easy welds, so that scarce master craftspeople are freed for the complex operations.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if I can build a robot that can do the simpler welds, it frees that company up to take their master welders to go work on the really hard weld, right?
claims.speaker: Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: Automating a restaurant dish room looks simple but is a hard robotics problem, because the system must both identify unsorted mixed items and adapt its grasp to each object type.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've not only got to figure out what's in the bucket, but you've got to be able to figure out how to grip a spoon versus a plate.
claims.speaker: Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: Stepper motors, their drivers and the surrounding circuits became dramatically cheaper over about a decade, which changed what a student robotics project can attempt even though the underlying motor technology is unchanged.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean, steppers are steppers and the drivers and all the circuits there are just incredibly cheap comparatively.
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: A robotics component company was founded to fill the gap between building every subsystem in-house and buying off-the-shelf parts that were designed for other markets, offering parts purpose-built for robotics but still flexible.
claims.quote_verbatim: I saw this gap in the market between, you know, building everything in house yourself or buying things off the shelf that were designed for other markets
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: How vertically integrated a robot must be depends on its size, weight and power budget: tight SWaP constraints force embedded, integrated designs that make off-the-shelf components and outside firms harder to bring in.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're really constrained in those regards, it's harder to integrate off the shelf components and you need to go to a more embedded and integrated design
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: Affordable 3D printing and free CAD tools in the mid-2010s became a common entry path into robotics, because the ability to design and modify parts rather than only print existing files is what pulls people into building machines.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd say in middle schools, when I really got into robotics, that was when I discovered 3D printing. So that was really when 3D printing started to take off like, you know, mid 2010s.
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa

attribution_notes: ep=59 passage is labeled speaker=Jeff Keyzer but the content is one of the two BeagleBoard guests answering a host question about what people build with BeagleBoard; it cannot be separated from Jason Kridner, so speaker is null.
ep=235 passage is labeled Matt Richardson but the ARMv7/ROS remarks alternate between host and guest inside one block; speaker left null.
ep=292 header says speaker=Chris Gammell, but the answer about motor accuracy and tolerances is the guest Timothy Lamb responding to the host's question, so it is attributed to Timothy Lamb.
ep=373 header says Chris Gammell, but the first-person passage about learning kinematics and drive mechanisms for career reasons is the other party in the exchange; speaker left null.

ep=407 passages carry mixed labels (Greg Charvat and Chris Gammell); the 10-meter free-space projection material is clearly Greg Charvat describing his own company's technology and is attributed to him.

ep=614 passages [99] and [102] are labeled Chris Gammell but the first-person content ('why I started capable robot components', the market-gap answer) belongs to guest Chris Osterwood; attributed to him.

ep=369, 405, 425, 437, 438, 495, 258 passages are flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE in the dump. In each case the first-person technical content matches the named guest describing their own work (Jason Huggins, Spencer Wright, Chris Osterwood, Chrissy Meyer, Bart Dring, Eric Klein, Bertrand Irrisou), and speakers were assigned by content rather than by label.

ep=121 passage flips between host questions and guest answers; the judgment that robotics technology is not yet capable of the manual assembly steps is attributed to Zach Hoeken as the person describing factory floors he had visited.
ep=116 speaker is a host reading a forum comment by Martin Ronin; the quote is attributed to Dave Jones as the reader, with the original source named in the claim text.
ep=411 passage alternates; the answers about calibration and manual datasheet lookup are Chris Denney describing his own assembly operation.
